definition: Exhaustive means covering every possible detail; thoroughly complete.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word exhaustive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know exhaustive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The detectives' sweep of the block was exhaustive — all fifty-one doors, including the three everyone swore stood empty.
A careful reader watches for errors; exhaustive promises far more — that every line, without exception, was checked.
Thorough work digs deep, but exhaustive goes to the end of the list: not most items, not nearly all — every one.

Comprehensive work takes in every major area of its subject — the whole scope, wall to wall. Exhaustive makes a harder claim: within that scope, every single item was reached. A comprehensive review covers every part of the curriculum; an exhaustive one accounts for every last worksheet.

Complete says the finished whole has nothing missing — no piece absent, no part unaccounted for. Exhaustive is that idea with a method attached: a sweep down the whole list, item by item, until nothing could be called skipped. A jigsaw is complete; a census is exhaustive.
covering only some of the ground
done at a pace that guarantees things get skipped

The root haust- ('to draw water') built exactly one family in English — exhaust and its offspring, exhaustive among them. Outside that family the root left nothing behind, so there is no cousin word to discover: the well, fittingly, is dry.
Exhaustive means covering every possible detail; thoroughly complete.
The used-bookshop's new owner spent her first March on an exhaustive count of the stock: every shelf, every cellar box, every paperback wedged behind the radiator.
Forty-one thousand titles later, she could say with a straight face that nothing in the building had escaped the ledger.
Exhaustive is the claim that nothing was left out — coverage complete down to the last item.
Its near-miss is exhausting, which describes fatigue.
March was surely both, but the count earns exhaustive because it reached everything, not because it wore anyone out.
Exhaustive makes a bold, checkable claim: everything was covered, without exception.
Say thorough when the work is deep but you can't vouch for every item, and keep exhausting for fatigue — the two get mixed up daily.
An exhaustive list is the one from which nothing could be called missing.

Every four years the state closes the Kestrel River bridge for a week and sends Rios's crew under it.
Their inspection is exhaustive by mandate: the checklist names all 3,112 rivets, every cable strand, each expansion joint, and the crew may not sign off while a single line remains unticked.
Most years a routine check would do — a walk of the deck, a look at the bearings, attention to the usual trouble spots.
But routine checks sample; they trust the spots between.
The four-year sweep trusts nothing.
The year the crew found the cracked pin, it was rivet number 2,977 — a part no sampling plan would ever have reached.
